channel.title: The Dig — HPC-QC integration and resource management
channel.description: Papers relevant to operating, benchmarking, integrating and using a semiconductor spin-qubit quantum computer of at least 16 qubits that is co-located with and integrated into an HPC system. Today's arXiv announcement, ranked against the HPC-QC integration and resource management preset. Today's ranked reading list centers on three high-relevance papers: 2611.27140 on FPGA-in-loop autonomous tuning of spin qubits, 2611.27927 on transpilation-aware multi-vendor QPU scheduling, and 2611.29983 on a calibration-aware quantum software stack. The remaining skims cover verified Hamiltonian-simulation compilation (2611.28388), semiclassical clustering for spin-ensemble decoherence (2611.28958), higher-order Trotter-Suzuki schemes (2611.27896), a binary-tree QAOA decomposition for Max k-Cut (2611.30508), and a learned small-circuit mitigation wrapper (2611.28261). item.title: Transpilation-Aware Multi-Vendor QPU Scheduling with Predicted Post-Transpilation Fidelity
item.description:
Read new method — Training-free topology-divergence estimate matches transpile-all device selection at about 25× lower latency, ranking measured success on IBM hardware at Spearman ρ=0.95 and reducing SLA violations from 42–74 jobs down to a few out of 102.

Grade 0.533 · 3.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Accelerating HPC With Quantum Computing: It Is a Software Challenge Too”

Figure

SLA violations (left) and false rejections (right) versus requested success probability τ for 102 jobs replayed on three IBM Heron devices. Filtering with the topology-divergence estimate keeps violations near zero, whereas raw-fidelity and random placement miss τ for 42 to 83 jobs.

Asks

Can a cluster scheduler automatically select the optimal QPU backend for a given quantum circuit to meet a target fidelity floor without running full transpilation on every candidate device?

Before

Selecting candidate QPUs by highest average device fidelity or via level-1 transpilation for every candidate device; picking by average fidelity produced 42–74 SLA violations out of 102 jobs.

But

Fails across vendors when published calibration figures overstate hardware fidelity (e.g., Rigetti Cepheus by 0.47, AQT IBEX Q1 by 0.25). Device-mean rates cannot differentiate near-identical devices or capture broad output distributions (such as QAOA and VQE). Tested on 6 devices across 4 vendors without neutral-atom targets.

Tools

topology-divergence estimate with VF2 subgraph embedding · two-stage schedule-reserve-transpile-bind protocol · Kubernetes and Slurm scheduling frameworks · Qiskit and tket compilers

Code. https://github.com/anapaulaappel/QPUScheduler

Abstract

Cluster schedulers already choose nodes, GPUs and accelerators for submitted workloads, enforce quotas and spread load. QPUs from several vendors are now schedulable resources in the same clusters, yet the user still names the device, usually the one with the best average fidelity. For a given circuit that choice is often wrong: compiling onto each device's qubit connectivity adds gates, so a job can meet its required success probability on one device and miss it on another with similar error rates, and checking this exactly by compiling for every candidate is too slow for a scheduling decision. We let the scheduler choose the QPU in two stages. A training-free estimate predicts, in milliseconds and without compiling, the success probability on every candidate and filters out those that would miss the requirement; only the chosen device then compiles the circuit, re-checks it, and binds the job or rolls back. The estimate matches compiling every candidate at about 25x lower latency in simulation, ranks measured success on IBM hardware as well as the post-compilation estimate (Spearman rho = 0.95), reduces requirement violations from tens of jobs to a few, and avoids them under contention without piling jobs onto one device. Across vendors it works when error rates are comparable (IBM and IQM) and fails when published figures overstate a device.

item.title: Cqlib: A High-Performance Software Stack for Quantum Computing
item.description:
Read new method — Cqlib 2.0 provides an end-to-end quantum computing software stack in native Rust with Python and C interfaces, verifying structural and semantic correctness across Benchpress parameterized compilation tasks while generating Quantum Control Instruction Set (QCIS) instructions for hardware execution.

Grade 0.658 · 5.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Integration of Quantum Accelerators with High Performance Computing—A Review of…”

Figure

The structural workflow showing program transformations from high-level circuit construction through Rust-based compilation down to QCIS hardware instructions and backend execution.

Asks

How can quantum programming workflows combine unified circuit semantics, multilingual high performance, and direct compilation to hardware-level control instruction sets like QCIS?

Before

Cqlib was previously a cloud-specific software interface restricted to supporting Tianyan Quantum Cloud experiments.

But

Evaluated only on the specific compilation and circuit-construction task scopes covered in Benchpress and reported test sets.

Tools

Rust core engine · Python and C FFI interfaces · Quantum Control Instruction Set (QCIS) · OpenQASM parser and generator · Benchpress benchmark suite

Abstract

This paper presents Cqlib, a high-performance software stack for quantum computing built around a unified quantum circuit model. Its native Rust core provides efficient implementations of circuit processing, quantum-state and operator computation, compilation, and optimization, while Python and C interfaces support algorithm development and system integration. Cqlib covers quantum program construction, simulation, analysis, compilation, device adaptation, and result processing under consistent program semantics. Through OpenQASM and the Quantum Control Instruction Set (QCIS), Cqlib supports program representation and hardware-oriented execution. Cqlib further provides backend interfaces for device execution, with Cqlib-Tianyan serving as one implementation for QCIS-compatible quantum hardware. Evaluations using parameterized compilation tasks from Benchpress and related tests show that Cqlib achieves good functional coverage, compilation correctness, and execution efficiency within the evaluated task scope. We develop Cqlib-Algorithm as a modular library of reusable operators and composable components for widely used quantum algorithms, including quantum search, phase estimation, and variational algorithms, with additional support for error mitigation. To complement these building blocks with domain-specific workflows, we further develop Cqlib-VQE, Cqlib-QAOA, and Cqlib-QML for application-level studies in quantum chemistry, combinatorial optimization, and quantum machine learning, respectively. Cqlib also integrates source-grounded Skills and MCP-based tools to support agent-assisted program generation, backend execution, and result-guided workflow refinement. Overall, Cqlib provides a unified and extensible software foundation that connects quantum algorithm development, simulation, compilation, and execution on QCIS-compatible quantum hardware.

item.title: Systematically improvable semiclassical clustering for accurate and efficient quantum dynamics in large spin ensembles
item.description:
Skim new method — Cluster spin-LSC reproduces numerically exact coherence revivals and population dynamics of spin sensors in many-spin baths, reducing multi-GPU runtimes from hours or days to minutes on a CPU.

Grade 0.486 · 3.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-Performance Computing with Quantum Processing Units”

Figure

Sensor coherence plotted against time under spin echo, CPMG-2, and CPMG-4 dynamical decoupling sequences. Plain semiclassics (Nc=0) misses revivals, while CSLSC systematically converges to exact SB-tMPS benchmarks as cluster size increases to Nc=8.

Asks

How can one accurately and efficiently simulate the decoherence of quantum spin sensors in realistic, strongly coupled nuclear spin baths under dynamical decoupling?

Before

Spin bath-truncated MPS (SB-tMPS) was limited to ∼200 bath spins and required hours on GPUs (Venkatesh 2024); semiclassical spin-LSC failed to reproduce entanglement-driven coherence revivals.

But

Infinite-temperature spin bath limit (kBT≫ℏω). Cluster exact diagonalization scales exponentially with the number of clustered bath spins (practical cluster size ∼14 spins).

Tools

Cluster spin-LSC (CSLSC) · Linearized semiclassical initial value representation (LSC-IVR) · SU(N) spin mapping · SB-tMPS benchmarks

Abstract

Predicting the decoherence of spin qubits in realistic environments is key to identifying the interactions that limit their coherence---a prerequisite for designing better quantum technologies. While accurate methods for spin dynamics are limited to relatively small systems, the dissipative spin environments in real experiments typically involve orders of magnitude more spins. Semiclassical methods can reach these sizes, but their classical treatment of the bath cannot capture the sensor-bath entanglement that generates coherence revivals, especially under the application of refocusing pulses. Here, we resolve this tension. We introduce cluster spin-LSC, a method that clusters the sensor together with a few strongly coupled bath spins, treating them quantum mechanically in an otherwise classical spin bath. We show that our method is applicable to systems containing arbitrary spin species under dynamical decoupling pulse sequences. Our method converges systematically to the exact dynamics with cluster size, providing an internal consistency check when no exact benchmarks exist. We demonstrate that cluster spin-LSC recovers numerically exact coherence and population dynamics for a nitrogen-vacancy center and a molecular qubit, reducing day-long multi-GPU simulations to only minutes on a CPU. We further extend our method to systems with large spin baths that lie beyond the reach of exact methods. Our approach thus offers a scalable and systematically improvable route to accurately simulate the decoherence dynamics of sensors in realistic spin environments.
